title: Neural Networks in Trading: Recurrent Modeling of Market Micromovements (Conclusion)
text:
Introduction
The market remains that same complex, multi-layered system where every micro-event — whether a spike in volume or a shift in the liquidity balance — forms its own trajectory. We observe this fabric of events every day, but few architectural solutions are capable of handling it as naturally as an event-driven neural network does. That is precisely why the
EV-MGRFlowNet
framework has become the foundation for developing a truly modern approach to analyzing market micromovements. In previous articles, we examined the key elements of the original architecture and adapted them to the specific requirements of financial time series, porting them to the
MQL5
environment using
OpenCL
. This approach is essential for achieving the ultimate goal — developing a model capable of perceiving the market as a stream of events in which the past and the present intertwine to form a single structure.
This perspective is closer to the classical interpretation of the behavior of a complex system, in which
price change as a process
takes center stage. It is here that the
EV-MGRFlowNet
architecture reveals its conceptual power. Its first major advantage is its ability to process data in event form, without requiring uniform sampling or fixed time windows. The market never moves at a steady pace: its rhythm is determined by surges of activity, lulls, and brief impulses, which, in the traditional approach, are lost between candlesticks. The event-driven model, on the other hand, reacts to every minor change as it occurs, rather than according to a predefined time grid, which makes it particularly expressive under actual price movement conditions.
Added to this is the depth of temporal memory provided by
FERE-Net
, which is based on
ConvGRU
and its modification,
ST-ConvGRU
. These mechanisms do more than simply collect information about the sequence of events. They maintain the structure of the unfolding movement, just as an experienced analyst tracks the overall kinematics of the process rather than momentary fluctuations. In a market where the direction of price movement is determined not by smooth trends but by chaotic bursts of liquidity, this memory becomes one of the architecture's key advantages. It is precisely because of this that the model does not lose context and can correctly interpret the sequence of market changes even when data density is high.
This dynamic is complemented by the multi-scale refinement implemented in
FGD-Net
. In the original architecture, it reconstructs optical flow at different resolution levels; in our financial context, it plays a similar role, allowing the model to reconstruct the direction and speed of market micromovements. This reconstruction views the market as a continuous vector process rather than a sequence of discrete points. Each new set of events refines the structure of the flow, creating a more coherent and stable description of the direction of movement. This makes it possible to analyze not only local spikes but also longer-lasting impulses. This is especially important for developing decision-making logic.
The
HMC-Loss
hybrid loss function plays an equally important role, as it allows the model to be trained without pre-prepared labels. For financial markets, where there is no single correct direction in the strict machine-learning sense, this property is crucial. The flow is assessed based on its internal temporal coherence, the smoothness of the reconstructed movement, and the internal connections between events. This approach naturally reduces the impact of random noise and highlights stable structures — the very ones that determine the actual dynamics of the market. Essentially, the model learns to distinguish between impulses that can develop into market movement and noise that should be ignored.
The authors’ visualization of the framework is shown below.
When porting the
EV-MGRFlowNet
architecture to
MQL5
, we faced not only the challenge of porting individual components but also the need to adapt the computational scheme itself. The implementation of
ST-ConvGRU
became the foundation upon which the entire framework is built. We have shown how to organize memory, how to maintain hidden states, and how to use
OpenCL
to process an event stream. These elements have formed a robust framework that enables the processing of large volumes of data while maintaining the architectural integrity of the model within a trading terminal environment.
A particular challenge was the absence of a spatial dimension in the financial data in the form typically used for computer vision tasks. Therefore, the multidimensionality of the original modules was reinterpreted through the structure of market data: event density, liquidity concentration, and the nature of aggressive and passive orders. This adaptation preserved the logic of the original architecture, allowing it to function in an environment where space is manifested not visually but structurally.
Today, we continue implementing the approaches proposed by the framework's authors using
MQL5
. At this stage, it is important for us not only to expand the architecture, but also to enable it to generate a meaningful description of market movements. While we previously focused on teaching the model
to perceive the flow of events
and
maintain its structure
through recurrent mechanisms, we are now taking the next step — moving on to reconstructing the market movement itself. This is precisely where the
FGD-Net
decoder comes into play — the very module that, in the original architecture, is responsible for multiscale refinement of the optical flow, and in our context becomes a tool for reconstructing the market dynamics vector.
Decoder
In the
EV-MGRFlowNet
architecture, the
decoder
plays a special role. It links the hidden states accumulated by the recurrent component to a specific prediction of the direction and intensity of motion, allowing the accumulated dynamics to be transformed into a form suitable for analysis. In other words,
FGD-Net
is a kind of lens through which the events collected by the model are transformed into a measurable and interpretable signal. That is exactly where we will begin our work today, examining the logic behind its design in detail and gradually adapting its architectural solutions to a format compatible with the capabilities of
MQL5
and
OpenCL
.
Before we get started, let's take another look at the authors’ visualization of the decoder modules.
At first glance, it seems like just another iteration of a recurrent convolutional unit, but if you look more closely, it becomes clear that there is a much more subtle logic underlying the interaction between the model’s levels.
First and foremost, it is worth paying attention to how the features fed into the recurrent block are generated. Unlike the traditional architecture, in which each layer of the decoder operates exclusively on its own output or on the result from the previous layer, this approach uses a projection of a
concatenated tensor
that combines two sources of information. The first source is the output of the previous decoder layer — that is, the dynamics that have already been partially reconstructed at a lower resolution. The second is the corresponding
encoder
level, which contains structural information about the original events that has not yet been processed through the multiscale reconstruction mechanisms. This combination produces a structurally rich input signal that contains both accumulated context and up-to-date information about the spatial and structural characteristics of the events being analyzed.
This combination is not merely a technical device, but a fundamentally important element of the entire architecture. The model can refine its motion estimate by continuously comparing the current reconstruction with the actual structure of the original flow. In classical optical flow problems, this helps prevent drift and stabilize the velocity field. In our context, this allows us to adjust the market micromovement vector based on the actual event structure.
The organization of the hidden state is no less interesting. In a standard
ConvGRU
, it is updated layer by layer. Each level of the decoder stores and uses its own memory. Here, however, the approach is entirely different — the hidden state represents
a projection of the entire model’s output
from the previous step, rather than the local state of a single layer. This solution brings the decoder closer to the concept of a global recurrent mechanism. The model does not rely on partial, disjointed states, but instead uses a unified dynamic flow derived in the previous step of sequence processing. In this way, the architecture prevents errors from accumulating between layers and maintains a coherent historical trajectory within a single recurrent context.
That is exactly what makes
FGD-Net
so expressive. The decoder functions as a multi-stage filter that compares its intermediate reconstructions with the global state of the model at each step. This results in a reliable and stable reconstruction of the direction of motion — whether it is the optical flow in the original problem or the market microflow in our port.
And once the overall logic of the calculations becomes clear enough, the time comes to translate the architectural concept from an abstract diagram into a concrete object. This is where a new module comes into play, combining the functions of the decoder and integrating the separate computational branches into a single, functional structure. We are designing it as a standalone component of the model — flexible enough to process complex tensor structures, and rigorous enough to meet the requirements of
OpenCL
computations.
This is how the
CNeuronFGDModule
class is created, fitting neatly into the existing structure.

Its design reflects the same architectural concept that we observed in the decoder graph. Individual submodules are responsible for normalization, convolutional transformations, feature formation, and recurrent dynamics, while the main object acts as the coordinator of all interactions.
Initializing the object was a natural extension of the architectural logic. Here, the sizes of the input and output spaces are specified, the channel structure is defined, a connection to the
OpenCL
context is established, and optimization modes are set. The multilayered structure of the computational graph we discussed earlier is now taking physical form. Each component knows its place and its role, and each is ready to fit into the overall computation cycle.
bool
CNeuronFGDModule::Init(
uint
numOutputs,
uint
myIndex, COpenCLMy *open_cl,
uint
units,
uint
main_dimension,
uint
flow_dimension,
uint
dimension_out,
                            ENUM_OPTIMIZATION optimization_type,
uint
batch)
  {
if
(!CNeuronBaseOCL::Init(numOutputs, myIndex, open_cl, units * dimension_out,
                            optimization_type, batch))
return
false
;
   activation = None;
As a first step, the module inherits the parameters of the base object. It is like the foundation on which the other components are built. Without a proper connection to the
OpenCL
context and correctly configured output channels, the rest of the logic simply cannot run. Next, top-level activation is disabled — it is important for the decoder to preserve purely numerical transformations without introducing nonlinearity where the framework's authors did not intend it.
Next, the step-by-step configuration of the internal components begins. We expect the module to receive a concatenated tensor at its input, formed from three data sources. Clearly, the values will have mismatched distributions, so we first use a batch normalization layer. It is responsible for aligning the scales of the feature maps.
uint
index =
0
;
if
(!cNorm.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, main_dimension * units, iBatch, optimization))
return
false
;
   cNorm.SetActivationFunction(None);
Its initialization determines the number of channels, which is equal to the product of the main stream's dimension and the number of unitary sequences — the very space where the features of the encoder and decoder intertwine. The absence of an activation function underscores its modest yet indispensable role: it does not alter the meaning of the data, but merely ensures its stability for subsequent operations.
Next, the convolutional layer
cD
comes into play. This is a tool that introduces dynamics into the module — it maps the local state and generates refined motion maps. The
TANH
activation function was chosen deliberately. In the context of
GRU
, it helps keep values within a limited range, maintaining stability when updating the hidden state.
index++;
if
(!cD.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, main_dimension, main_dimension, dimension_out, units,
1
, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cD.SetActivationFunction(TANH);
Next, the flow projection block is initialized; it serves as a sort of gateway between the state of previous steps and the current computations.
index++;
if
(!cFlowIn.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, flow_dimension * units, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   DeleteObj(cFlowIn.getOutput())
   cFlowIn.SetActivationFunction(None);
   index++;
if
(!cFlow.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, flow_dimension, flow_dimension, dimension_out, units,
1
, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cFlow.SetActivationFunction(None);
A little further on, a feature concatenation object (
cConcatenated
) is created. It is especially important here that the dimensions match exactly, because even the slightest discrepancy will instantly destroy the entire computational graph.
index++;
if
(!cConcatenated.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL,
2
* dimension_out * units, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cConcatenated.SetActivationFunction(None);
And the finishing touch — the multichannel convolution
cXH
. It serves as the computational core of the
ConvGRU
mechanism: this is where the projections of the analyzed features and the hidden state are generated. A pair of windows of the same size creates a symmetrical structure, and the total number of output channels — three times the width of the output dimension — reflects the three core elements of the
GRU
algorithm.
index++;
uint
windows[] = { dimension_out, dimension_out };
if
(!cXH.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, windows,
3
* dimension_out, units,
1
, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
   cXH.SetActivationFunction(None);
//---
return
true
;
  }
No activation, no frills — just pure math.
Once all submodules have been initialized, the FGD module is now a unified architectural unit in which each element performs its own function, adhering to the order and structure established in the original model. And it is precisely this accuracy, this harmony of its internal structure, that makes it the foundation for the subsequent implementation of recurrent logic and the reconstruction of a multiscale motion field.
After initializing the object, we proceed to implement the forward pass algorithm in the
feedForward
method which follows the strict, deterministic data processing sequence characteristic of the
EV-MGRFlowNet
architecture.
bool
CNeuronFGDModule::feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL, CBufferFloat *SecondInput)
  {
if
(!cFlowIn.SetOutput(SecondInput,
false
))
return
false
;
The module receives pointers to two sources of input data as parameters. One of them is represented by a buffer object. However, the architecture of the object's internal components calls for the use of only neural layers; therefore, as our first operation, we set the obtained pointer as the result buffer of a specially created object.
The next step is data normalization. The normalization layer evens out the distribution of input values, ensuring the stability of subsequent layers and improving training efficiency. An error at this stage causes the method to terminate immediately.
if
(!cNorm.FeedForward(NeuronOCL))
return
false
;
After normalization, the data is passed to the
cD
block. This component acts as a transformation layer that performs convolutional filtering operations and generates an initial feature map.
if
(!cD.FeedForward(cNorm.AsObject()))
return
false
;
In parallel, a second data stream is processed through
cFlow,
which projects the global hidden state into the feature space of the current layer.
if
(!cFlow.FeedForward(cFlowIn.AsObject()))
return
false
;
Next, the results of both streams are concatenated.
if
(!Concat(cD.getOutput(), cFlow.getOutput(), cConcatenated.getOutput(),
              cD.GetFilters(), cFlow.GetFilters(), cFlow.GetUnits()))
return
false
;
The combined data is passed to the
cXH
layer. It projects the features being analyzed and the hidden state into the quantities required to perform the operations of the
GRU
algorithm. Using the multi-window convolution object allows us to generate all these quantities simultaneously in parallel threads within the
OpenCL
context.
if
(!cXH.FeedForward(cConcatenated.AsObject()))
return
false
;
A key step in the forward pass is the call to the
GRU
method, where recurrent processing of temporal dependencies takes place. The
GRU
enables the module to account for sequences of events over time, which is critical for analyzing financial data. Any error at this step stops the method.
if
(!GRU())
return
false
;
Before the method completes, we set the gradients of the
cD
block to zero. This operation ensures that previously accumulated gradient values will not affect subsequent training iterations, keeping the computations clean.
if
(!cD.getGradient().Fill(
0
))
return
false
;
//---
return
true
;
  }
If all steps are completed successfully, the method returns
true
, confirming that the forward pass was executed correctly. Taken together, this sequence reflects the key principles of the
EV-MGRFlowNet
architecture: clear modularity, state control for each block, and optimization of computational resources.
The
calcInputGradients
method implements a key component of the training process for the
CNeuronFGDModule
module — the backpropagation algorithm. While the forward pass organizes the flow of information through the network, backpropagation is responsible for adjusting the parameters and allows the model to gradually converge toward the desired results.
bool
CNeuronFGDModule::calcInputGradients(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL,
                                          CBufferFloat *SecondInput,
                                          CBufferFloat *SecondGradient,
                                          ENUM_ACTIVATION SecondActivation = None)
  {
if
(!NeuronOCL || !SecondGradient)
return
false
;
The method begins by verifying the validity of the pointers to the source data objects. Without them, further calculations are impossible. This is a basic but critically important safeguard against errors.
Next, we synchronize the pointers to the gradient buffer of the second data stream and a specially created internal object.
if
(!cFlowIn.SetGradient(SecondGradient,
true
))
return
false
;
   cFlowIn.SetActivationFunction(SecondActivation);
Next, the error gradient is backpropagated through the recurrent block. This is where the gradients of the recurrent connections are computed, which allows us to account for the effect of temporal dependencies on the model's error.
if
(!GRU_grad())
return
false
;
The next step is to compute the hidden gradients of the combined buffer. The method correctly distributes the error among the combined streams, preparing the data for separate processing.
if
(!cConcatenated.CalcHiddenGradients(cXH.AsObject()))
return
false
;
The
DeConcat
operation splits the combined gradient into parts corresponding to the
cD
and
cFlow
layers. The filter parameters and sequence dimensionality ensure the correct partitioning of multidimensional data.
if
(!DeConcat(cD.getPrevOutput(), cFlow.getGradient(), cConcatenated.getGradient(),
                cD.GetFilters(), cFlow.GetFilters(), cFlow.GetUnits()))
return
false
;
Next, the gradient of the
cD
object is summed. This step allows us to combine the values of the two data streams and stabilize the training process.
if
(!SumAndNormilize(cD.getGradient(), cD.getPrevOutput(), cD.getGradient(), cD.GetFilters(),
false
,
0
,
0
,
0
,
1
))
return
false
;
The
Deactivation
method correctly adjusts the resulting gradient values using the derivatives of the corresponding activation functions.
Deactivation(cFlow)
   Deactivation(cD)
Next, we correctly propagate the gradients of the two data streams back to the source data.
if
(!cFlowIn.CalcHiddenGradients(cFlow.AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!cNorm.CalcHiddenGradients(cD.AsObject()))
return
false
;
if
(!NeuronOCL.CalcHiddenGradients(cNorm.AsObject()))
return
false
;
//---
return
true
;
  }
If all steps were completed successfully, the method returns
true
, indicating that the gradients were calculated correctly.
Taken together, this sequence reflects fine-grained control over error distribution and demonstrates the modular, robust architecture of
EV-MGRFlowNet
, in which each component performs its specific task and ensures stable model training.
Thus, the
FGD
module becomes not just a part of the architecture, but also a bridge between theory and practice. It adopts the same structural choices as the original model, but expresses them in a form compatible with the
MQL5
and
OpenCL
environments. And it is precisely at this stage that it becomes clear: the decoder is not just a formality, but the key to enabling the model to reconstruct motion in all its multiscale complexity.
Top-level object
Following the successful implementation of individual modules of the
EV-MGRFlowNet
framework, the next key step is to integrate all components into a single, cohesive structure. This role is fulfilled by the
CNeuronEVMGRFlowNet
class, which inherits basic functionality from
CNeuronSpikeActivation
and combines an
encoder
, a
central block
, and a
decoder
, providing a complete information processing cycle from the model’s input to its output.
class
CNeuronEVMGRFlowNet  :
public
CNeuronSpikeActivation

Within the class, we see three main components:
cEncoder
(
CNeuronFERENet
) — acts as a feature encoder and translates the analyzed data into the model's internal representation;
cNeck
(
CNeuronSTEFlowNetResidualBlock
) — serves as the central residual processing block, enabling deep extraction and transformation of hidden features;
cDecoder
— maps the transformed representation back into the output data space.
This division illustrates the modular approach of
EV-MGRFlowNet
, in which each block is responsible for a strictly defined task, and their integration ensures the coordinated operation of the entire model.
The
Init
method performs a comprehensive initialization of all the class's internal components, ensuring structural consistency and correct model operation at every level. This is a key step in building the complete architecture — from the encoder to the decoder — ready for training and a forward pass.
bool
CNeuronEVMGRFlowNet::Init(
uint
numOutputs,
uint
myIndex, COpenCLMy *open_cl,
uint
units,
uint
&chanels[],
                               ENUM_OPTIMIZATION optimization_type,
uint
batch)
  {
if
(chanels.Size() <
2
)
return
false
;
if
(!CNeuronSpikeActivation::Init(numOutputs, myIndex, open_cl, units * chanels[
0
], optimization_type, batch))
return
false
;
First, the method checks that the input channel array
chanels
is valid — the array must contain at least two elements. This ensures that the network will have both incoming and outgoing data flows. If the condition is not met, initialization is aborted.
Next, the method of the same name in the parent class is called to initialize the basic functionality and configure the object's fundamental settings, including resource allocation and memory for computations.
The number of layers in the encoder and decoder is set to one less than the number of elements in the channel array.
uint
layers = chanels.Size() -
1
;
Next, the encoder is created and initialized. It receives the parameters provided by the user.
//--- Encoder
int
index =
0
;
if
(!cEncoder.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, units, chanels, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
Successful initialization of the encoder ensures that the internal data representation is formed correctly.
The next step is to initialize the central block
cNeck,
which is responsible for deep feature extraction and provides the residual connections necessary for stable training of the deep model.
index++;
if
(!cNeck.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, chanels[layers], units,
32
,
8
, optimization, iBatch))
return
false
;
Next, let's move on to working with the decoder. First, the dynamic array of objects is cleared and a pointer to the
OpenCL
object is passed; then, the construction of the data reconstruction layers begins.
//--- Decoder
cDecoder.Clear();
   cDecoder.SetOpenCL(OpenCL);
   CNeuronFGDModule* fgd =
NULL
;
   CNeuronBaseOCL*   concat = cNeck.AsObject();
uint
flow_dimension = chanels[
0
];
At each stage, a new
CNeuronFGDModule
is created with parameters corresponding to the dimensions of the previous layer (
main_dimension
), the flow size (
flow_dimension
), and the number of outputs of the current layer. After successful initialization, the module is added to the decoder.
for
(
uint
i =
0
; i < layers; i++)
     {
uint
main_dimension = concat.Neurons() / units;
      fgd =
new
CNeuronFGDModule();
if
(!fgd ||
         !fgd.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, units, main_dimension, flow_dimension, chanels[layers - i -
1
],
                                                                            optimization, iBatch) ||
         !cDecoder.Add(fgd))
        {
         DeleteObj(fgd)
return
false
;
        }
Special attention has been paid to ensuring that the layers are combined correctly. If a corresponding encoder layer exists for the current level, a
concat
object is created that concatenates the neurons from the decoder, block
D
of the current module, and the encoder.
if
(i == (layers -
1
))
break
;
      index++;
      CNeuronBaseOCL* encoder = cEncoder.GetLayer(-
int
(i +
1
));
      CNeuronBaseOCL* d = fgd.GetD();
if
(!encoder)
        {
         concat =
new
CNeuronBaseOCL();
if
(!concat ||
            !concat.Init(
0
, index, OpenCL, fgd.Neurons() + d.Neurons(), optimization, iBatch) ||
            !cDecoder.Add(concat))
           {
            DeleteObj(concat)
return
false
;
           }
        }
else
{
         concat =
new
CNeuronBaseOCL();
if
(!concat ||
            !concat.Init(

from

through

the Actor
and

MetaTrader
5 Strategy Tester. The luxury of calmly working with historical data is now gone. Each candlestick is like a real-time market reaction. The model reacts instantly, analyzes fluctuations caused by noise, adapts to sudden spikes, and adjusts its actions during periods of low liquidity.
EV-MGRFlowNet
acts as an invisible mentor, keeping the network from making mistakes and advising it when to act boldly and when to exercise caution. The underlying structure, built on historical data, remains its foundation, but the model now learns to respond flexibly to the current situation, much like a trader with live trading experience.
The final exam is testing the model on new data from
July through September 2025

The test results show steady, stable performance. The equity curve rises steadily, without sharp spikes or erratic fluctuations. The balance and equity move almost in tandem, as if they were two coordinated mechanisms. One supports the strategy's underlying logic, while the other reflects the current status of open positions. Together, they produce smooth growth that feels neither random nor forced. The resulting growth — from USD 100.0 to USD 126.81 — appears to be a natural outcome of the algorithm's operation, rather than a consequence of random fluctuations.
This smoothness is supported by quantitative data. A profit factor of 1.51 and a recovery factor of 1.32 indicate that the strategy not only generates profits more often than losses, but also recovers steadily from drawdowns. The average profit per trade of USD 1.28 is not generated by isolated spikes but through consistent, steady movement, which makes the outcome more predictable.
Drawdowns are viewed as natural fluctuations. The maximum balance drawdown of USD 16.40 (12.68%) and maximum equity drawdown of USD 20.25 (15.44%) are not cause for concern, since the equity hardly deviates from the balance. This means that open positions do not remain in the red or place a prolonged strain on margin, and the chart clearly shows that small declines are quickly followed by consecutive gains.
The trading structure demonstrates the algorithm's internal harmony. Of the 21 trades, about 57% were profitable, and the distribution of short and long positions appears balanced. This indicates that the strategy is not fixated on a single market phase and can adapt to various conditions, whether momentum moves or periods of sideways trading.
Monitoring the equity curve and deposit load shows disciplined trading with a low leverage ratio. The deposit load rarely exceeds a few percent and generally remains within the 1–5% range. The algorithm does not take an overly aggressive approach to the market; it acts decisively, but within the defined risk limits.
Ultimately, the backtesting reveals a comprehensive, consistent picture: the algorithm steadily grows the capital, keeps drawdowns under control, and consistently generates profits.
Conclusion
We have completed the implementation of the approaches proposed by the authors of the
EV-MGRFlowNet
framework. The implemented solution demonstrates a high degree of architectural coherence, resilience to market fluctuations, and the ability to develop strategies independently. Integrating all components — the encoder, the central unit, and the decoder — into a single structure has made it possible to create a model that manages capital smoothly and predictably, minimizing stressful drawdowns and maintaining control over risks.
Testing showed that the strategy performs in a balanced manner. Profits are generated systematically, without relying on isolated successful trades, and backpropagation mechanisms ensure that the weights are consistently updated and that the model remains adaptive. The profit factor, recovery factors, and geometric return metrics confirm the effectiveness and reliability of the model.

against: The article describes a neural network architecture (EV-MGRFlowNet) trained end-to-end on financial time series, but it never specifies *how the trading signal is generated* — i.e., there is no explicit rule defining when to enter/exit trades. It only states that the model 'reconstructs the market dynamics vector' and 'feeds into the Actor and Critic', but gives no formula, threshold, condition, or decision logic linking the decoder output (e.g., reconstructed flow vector) to a concrete trade (buy/sell/hold). This violates criterion (2): 'rule cannot be written as a precise formula because article gives only general description or architecture without entry conditions.'

The model is described as 'event-driven' and processes 'a stream of events', but the article does not define what constitutes an 'event' in spot forex (e.g., tick-level price change? volume spike? order book delta?), nor does it specify how events are sourced or timestamped. Crucially, it mentions adaptation 'to the structure of market data: event density, liquidity concentration, and the nature of aggressive and passive orders' — the latter two ('aggressive/passive orders', 'liquidity concentration') require order book data (Level 2/3), which is *not available in standard spot forex* (only bid/ask quotes, no real volumes or full depth). This violates criterion (3): 'needs data which does not exist for spot forex (order book, real volumes, etc.)'.
non_fatal: No out-of-sample test details beyond 'July–September 2025' are provided (e.g., walk-forward protocol, robustness across instruments or volatility regimes).
No mention of spread, slippage, or commission modeling in testing — but per instructions, this is non-fatal.

Training uses reinforcement learning ('Actor'/'Critic'), but the reward function, action space discretization, or policy extraction mechanism is not specified — however, this is not a fatal flaw *if* a deterministic signal can still be derived; the fatal issue is the absence of any stated signal logic.
The equity curve and metrics (profit factor, drawdown) are reported, but no statistical significance (e.g., Monte Carlo shuffle, bootstrap p-value) is given — non-fatal per instructions.

judge.reject_reason: Статья описывает архитектуру нейросетевой модели EV-MGRFlowNet и её реализацию в MQL5, но не содержит чёткого, детерминированного правила входа: не указано, как именно выход декодера (вектор микродвижения рынка) преобразуется в торговый сигнал (long/short). Нет ни порогов, ни условий, ни формул, ни логики перевода выходного тензора в направление сделки. Также модель опирается на данные, недоступные на стандартных спот-форекс-барах: 'aggressive and passive orders', 'liquidity concentration' — это элементы стакана (Level 2/3), отсутствующие в обычных котировках spot forex. Это фатальный порок: правило невозможно записать, а требуемые данные неприменимы.
judge.author_oos_metrics: Рост капитала с 100.0 до 126.81 USD, profit factor 1.51, recovery factor 1.32, средняя прибыль на сделку 1.28 USD, максимальный просадок баланса 12.68%, 57% прибыльных сделок за период июля–сентября 2025 года.
judge.summary: Статья представляет архитектуру EV-MGRFlowNet — event-driven нейросети для реконструкции микродвижений рынка, адаптированной к MQL5 через OpenCL. Она подробно описывает модули (FERE-Net, FGD-Net, HMC-Loss), их инициализацию и обучение, но полностью опускает логику генерации торговых сигналов. Нет ни одного условия входа, порога, формулы или описания, как выход модели преобразуется в решение 'купить' или 'продать'.
